title: Quantum Startup Qarakal Takes Lessons From Classical Systems With Pangaea Architecture
gist: Israeli quantum startup Qarakal has unveiled Pangaea, a superconducting quantum architecture built around a 'quantum bus' that lets logical qubits with different error-correction codes connect without physical adjacency, which the company claims needs only a tenth of the physical qubits of conventional monolithic quantum architectures.

themes.theme: Architecture as quantum computing's maturity phase

insights.claim: Qarakal co-founder and CTO Nadav Katz argues the quantum computing industry is entering a maturity phase defined by systems architecture rather than raw qubit accumulation, drawing a direct analogy to classical computing's shift from Turing's unstructured 'pile of bits' to the specialized, communication-based Von Neumann architecture that classical computers still use today.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Investors should treat architecture-focused quantum vendors (not just qubit-count leaders) as a distinct competitive category, since the founder's framing implies qubit count alone will not determine commercial winners.
insights.quote: What really worked was the Von Neumann architecture, which basically is – with some very interesting recent modifications – what we use to this day, eighty years later.
insights.locator: The architecture work signals a growing maturity in the quantum space

insights.claim: Katz characterizes the dominant current quantum computing approach as a 'monolithic architecture' — a single large, adjacency-dependent array of qubits programmed after the fact — and frames this as the industry's core unsolved problem ('the current boogeyman of quantum computing'), positioning Qarakal against this prevailing design pattern.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A direct critique of the industry-standard monolithic qubit-array approach signals where Qarakal expects incumbents to hit scaling limits, useful for benchmarking rival vendors' architectures against this specific failure mode.
insights.quote: The current boogeyman of quantum computing is this sort of monolithic architecture in which you just say, 'Let's just have this huge sort of planar thing that grows maybe by chiplets being connected, but ultimately, it's just a huge array of qubits that you just program after the fact to do something.

insights.claim: Qarakal argues that current quantum systems require logical qubits to be physically adjacent and each qubit to perform every function (computation, communication, and error correction simultaneously), which tightly couples these functions and prevents components from scaling independently, making conventional quantum architectures costly and hard to scale.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific structural cost driver (forced physical adjacency and function-coupling) in incumbent quantum architectures that investors can use as a checklist item when assessing competing vendors' scalability claims.
insights.locator: Current quantum systems are complex monoliths

insights.claim: Qarakal's Pangaea architecture is built around a 'quantum bus,' a communication interface analogous to a classical computer's bus or backplane, that lets logical qubits using different error-correction codes and module types connect and perform fault-tolerant logical operations without needing to be physically adjacent.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: The quantum bus is the specific mechanism underlying Qarakal's scalability and cost claims; its real-world performance is the key technical risk to monitor as the company moves toward deployment.
insights.locator: The Qarakal quantum bus is a foundational element of Pangaea

insights.claim: Qarakal's director of quantum software Sheir Yarkoni says the quantum bus removes the current tradeoff between error-correction codes with high encoding rates (fewer physical qubits per logical qubit, but costly connectivity and operations) and simpler, more scalable planar codes (easier to operate, but requiring more physical qubits per logical qubit), by letting both coexist as specialized modules in one system rather than forcing a single code choice.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Analogous to classical computing's storage-hierarchy design (fast/small vs. slow/dense), this suggests Qarakal is targeting a heterogeneous, tiered quantum memory/compute architecture rather than a uniform qubit fabric — a design pattern to watch for in competitors too.
insights.quote: If you have a unit that you want to build that has a high density of memory and slower operations – like what we would think of as a hard disk in a classical computer – and you have another code that's very lightweight and has fast operations, but it doesn't have a lot of memory – kind of the equivalent of RAM in classical computing – then we don't want to build a computer where you have to choose between those.

insights.claim: Katz says the quantum bus produces a slower accumulation of errors than conventional monolithic architectures, which allows smaller logical qubits (fewer physical qubits needed per logical qubit) and, in turn, faster convergence toward fault tolerance.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: This is Qarakal's core technical bet: slower error accumulation as the mechanism for both cost reduction and faster fault-tolerance timelines — a testable claim to track against independent benchmarks once systems ship.
insights.quote: Here you get more logical operations out of the qubits that are there, so it's just that much more efficient and converges to fault tolerance faster.

insights.claim: Qarakal claims its Pangaea/quantum-bus architecture requires only a tenth of the physical qubits that conventional monolithic architectures need for equivalent logical capability, which Katz says translates into less infrastructure overall, including less wiring, lower energy consumption, and less noise.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A claimed 10x reduction in physical-qubit requirements is a headline, order-of-magnitude cost and resource claim that would materially change the capex case for fault-tolerant quantum computing if independently validated — a key metric to watch for third-party verification.
insights.quote: the Pangaea architecture requires a 10th of the physical qubits that other approaches need
insights.locator: The quantum bus has an immediate tangible benefit

insights.claim: Katz attributes much of the physical-qubit overhead in conventional monolithic architectures to qubits spending effort 'shuttling things around' rather than performing logical operations, which reduces the error-correction threshold and makes fault tolerance harder to reach.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Pinpoints qubit shuttling overhead as a specific, quantifiable inefficiency in rival monolithic architectures that Qarakal's design claims to eliminate.
insights.quote: a lot of the [qubit] effort is just shuttling things around. That creates an overhead and reduces the threshold and makes it harder to achieve fault tolerance.

insights.claim: Qarakal Quantum is a superconducting-qubit quantum computing startup founded in 2024 in Israel, and its Pangaea architecture and quantum bus were recently unveiled as part of a three-step roadmap: 2026 focused on integrating components and capabilities, system deployments targeted for 2028, and further system expansion two years after that.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Gives investors concrete, dated milestones (2028 deployment target) to check Qarakal's execution against as a young, well-funded-sounding but pre-deployment quantum startup.
insights.locator: The introduction of the Pangaea architecture and quantum bus is part of a three-step roadmap

themes.theme: A broader industry race on architecture

insights.claim: Qarakal's architecture push is part of a broader industry trend of quantum vendors focusing on system architecture rather than raw qubit counts: D-Wave is developing a dual-rail superconducting architecture, and QuiX Quantum introduced its Dedalo architecture for fault-tolerant photonics systems alongside its Carina commercial system.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Signals that architecture-level differentiation (not just qubit count or modality) is becoming a competitive battleground across multiple quantum computing vendors and modalities (superconducting, photonic, annealing) simultaneously, worth tracking as a cross-vendor theme.
